topics.title: Accountability Basics: Scope, Autonomy, and Governance
topics.summary: Accountability means answering for what you do, decide, and fail to do, built on five professional components and on practicing to the full extent of your license.
objectives: You can tell accountability apart from responsibility, authority, and liability.
You can explain top-of-license practice and its two limits.
You can compare professional and individual autonomy.
You can name who sets nursing rules and which source wins.
You can match a nurse’s behavior to one of the five components.
You can pick the accountable action when pressure conflicts with client safety.
topics.bigPicture:
Accountability is one simple promise: “I will answer for what I do, what I decide, and what I fail to do.” You may need to explain a choice to the client, your employer, the board of nursing, or a court. It is not about blame. It is about ownership.

This idea sits under most Management of Care questions on the NCLEX. You can hand a task to someone else. You cannot hand off your judgment or your duty to follow up. This lesson covers the key words, top-of-license practice, autonomy, governance, and the five components of accountability.
recap: Accountability means answering for your judgments, actions, omissions, and outcomes. Responsibility is the duty to do a task.
You can delegate a task, but never your accountability for the judgment and follow-up.
Top-of-license practice uses your full education and legal scope—never beyond your scope or competence.
Professional autonomy is nursing regulating itself; individual autonomy is your freedom to act within scope.
Governance—boards, professional groups, shared governance—gives nurses control over practice, discipline, and working conditions.
Five components: education, body of knowledge, service orientation, code of ethics, and autonomy through professional organizations.
Facility policy can narrow your scope but never widen it past the Nurse Practice Act.
Accountable pattern: assess, act within scope, communicate, document truthfully, report and follow up.

keyTerms.def: Answering for your own nursing judgments, actions, omissions, and their results. It cannot be passed to someone else.
The duty to carry out a task. A task can be assigned or delegated.
The rightful power to act or direct others, from your license and job position.
Legal responsibility for harm, decided after the fact by a court or board.
Practicing to the full extent of your education, skills, and legal scope. It came from the IOM’s 2010 Future of Nursing report.
What a nurse may legally do, set by the state Nurse Practice Act and board of nursing rules.
Nursing’s power to regulate itself: set standards, write policy, and define its roles and scope through state boards of nursing.
Your freedom to perform needed nursing actions within scope, while answering for them and advocating for safe care.
Structure from professional nursing organizations that lets nurses control their practice, self-discipline, and working conditions.
A facility model where bedside nurses share decisions about practice, quality, and staffing through councils.
The state law that defines nursing, sets legal scope, and creates the board of nursing.
The state agency that licenses, writes rules, investigates, and disciplines nurses to protect the public.
NCSBN is the group of state boards that writes the NCLEX. The ANA is a professional group that writes the Code of Ethics.
Care that blends the best research, your clinical expertise, and the client’s values and preferences.
Charting something untrue, such as care not done or a false time. It is never acceptable.

sections.heading: What is accountability?
sections.keyIdea: Accountability means you answer for your judgments, actions, and omissions—and you cannot hand it to anyone else.
sections.body:
Accountability means answering for what you do and decide. It also covers what you fail to do. A missed step is an omission, and it counts.

Three look-alike words cause confusion. Responsibility is the duty to do a task. Authority is the right to act or direct others. Liability is legal blame for harm, decided later.

A task can be handed off. Accountability for nursing judgment stays with the licensed nurse. If an RN asks an assistant to take vital signs, the assistant must measure and report them. The RN still must give clear directions and act on the results. “I delegated it” is not a defense.

You answer to the client first, then to yourself, the profession, your employer, and the law. When these conflict, client safety wins.

rows: Right to act or direct others
Decided later by a court or board

check.q: An assistant charts a postoperative BP of 84/50 but tells no one. Two hours later the client is drowsy and hypotensive. Who was accountable for acting on it?
check.a: The RN keeps accountability for follow-up. The assistant was responsible, and accountable, for reporting the value as directed. The RN was accountable for clear reporting rules, checking results, and acting. Delegation moves the task, not the RN’s accountability.

sections.heading: What is top-of-license practice?
sections.keyIdea: Top-of-license practice means doing all the nursing work your education and legal scope allow—never less, and never more.
sections.body:
Top-of-license (TOL) practice is an interprofessional way of delivering care. It means each team member works at the highest level their training and legal scope allow. It grew from the Institute of Medicine’s 2010 report, The Future of Nursing: Leading Change, Advancing Health.

Why does it matter? When RNs spend the shift on tasks others could do, RN-only work gets skipped. That includes assessment, teaching, care coordination, and evaluation. The course lists eight core RN duties in TOL. It highlights outcomes-focused care and safe transitions, such as handoffs and discharges.

TOL includes a duty to advocate for your own and colleagues’ autonomy. It also has two ceilings: your legal scope and your personal competence. Practicing at the top of your license is the opposite of practicing beyond it.

Course vs current: Your course guide says TOL lets nurses with a BSN or higher practice to the fullest extent of their education, skills, and legal scope. Current standard: the 2010 report says every nurse should practice to the full extent of his or her own education and training. On a course exam, expect the BSN wording. On the NCLEX, apply TOL to any RN.
sections.example: RNs spend each morning restocking carts while clients wait for reassessment after opioids. A TOL-minded nurse brings data to the practice council and asks that support staff restock.

check.q: Which reflects TOL practice: passing every meal tray yourself, or coordinating discharge teaching for a client going home on new insulin?
check.a: Coordinating discharge teaching. Safe transitions and teaching need RN judgment. Others can pass trays.

sections.heading: What does autonomy mean in nursing?
sections.keyIdea: The profession regulates itself, and each nurse acts independently within scope—both must answer for their choices.
sections.body:
Autonomy means independence. In nursing it works at two levels.

Professional autonomy belongs to nursing as a whole. The profession regulates itself. It sets standards, writes nursing policy, and defines its scope. The legal power sits with state boards of nursing.

Individual autonomy is yours at the bedside. You may perform needed nursing actions within scope, like repositioning, teaching, or holding an opioid when breathing is slow. Freedom comes paired with answerability. The more you decide, the more you must explain and document.

On the NCLEX, autonomy appears as the option where the nurse acts within scope instead of waiting for permission.
sections.analogy: A sports league writes the rulebook and disciplines players. That is professional autonomy. Each player chooses how to play within the rules and answers for each play. That is individual autonomy.

rows: Standards, policy, and discipline through boards
Nursing judgments and actions within scope
Scope, competence, medical orders, and the client’s own choices

check.q: A client is hard to arouse with a respiratory rate of 9 after an opioid. The next dose is due. What shows accountable individual autonomy?
check.a: Hold the dose, stimulate and reassess breathing and sedation, follow the respiratory depression protocol, notify the provider, and document.

sections.heading: Who sets the rules for nursing?
sections.keyIdea: Governance is how nurses control their own practice, discipline, and working conditions—through boards, professional groups, and unit councils.
sections.body:
Governance is the structure that lets nurses run their own professional affairs. Per the course, professional nursing organizations provide it. It sets up social, political, and economic arrangements so nurses control their practice, self-discipline, and working conditions.

It works at the state, national, and facility levels, as the table shows. At work, shared governance councils let bedside nurses help shape policy.

“Who decides?” questions are governance questions. The board decides what is legal. Facility policy can be stricter than the law, but never looser. To change a unit practice, bring evidence to the practice council. Do not quietly ignore policy.

rows: Group of boards; writes the NCLEX and model rules
Code of Ethics; scope and standards
Local rules; may be stricter than law
How a task is done here

check.q: Nurses on a unit co-sign wastes they did not witness “to save time.” What should a new nurse do?
check.a: Refuse to co-sign, since that is falsification and a diversion risk. Follow policy, then raise the issue with the manager and practice council.

sections.heading: What are the five components?
sections.keyIdea: Five components make nursing an accountable profession: education, a body of knowledge, service, a code of ethics, and professional organization.
sections.body:
The course names five components that promote professional accountability. Exam stems describe a behavior and ask which component it shows. So learn what each one looks like.

The course guide labels component 1 “Education (Body of Knowledge)” and component 2 “Body of Knowledge.” Treat them as two items: learning that gets you licensed, and the knowledge base of the profession.

Course vs current: Your course guide lists MSN and doctorate (DNP/PhD) programs as ways into practice. Current standard: a first RN license comes from an approved diploma, ADN, BSN, or entry-level master’s program, plus the NCLEX-RN. A DNP or PhD is almost always an advanced degree for nurses who are already RNs. On a course exam, expect all five program types. On the NCLEX, every route ends with passing the NCLEX-RN.

Course vs current: Your course guide says nursing codes of ethics are “regulated alongside state boards of nursing via the NCSBN.” Current standard: the ANA writes and updates the Code of Ethics for Nurses. The NCSBN does not write or regulate it. Boards enforce the Nurse Practice Act and may discipline unethical conduct. On a course exam, expect the NCSBN wording. On the NCLEX, the Code belongs to the ANA.
bullets: Education. Entry needs an approved nursing program plus passing the NCLEX. The course lists five program types: hospital diploma, associate degree (ADN), bachelor’s (BSN), master’s (MSN), and doctorate (DNP or PhD). The ANA recommends the BSN for entry. Many ADN nurses go on through RN-to-BSN programs. Seen as: starting an RN-to-BSN program or earning a certification.

Body of knowledge. Nursing’s own distinct, ever-growing knowledge, built on nursing frameworks and ongoing research. Nurses apply it through evidence-based practice (EBP) to keep care safe. Seen as: checking current evidence before changing a routine.

Service orientation. Unlike jobs driven by profit, nursing puts service to others first, based on tradition and accountability. Rules, policies, and codes of ethics guide it. Seen as: volunteering in a state or national Medical Reserve Corps during a crisis like COVID-19. Volunteers help local health departments with data collection, phone banks, and public health information.

Code of ethics. Respecting the inherent worth and dignity of all people. Doing what is right, even at personal cost, to keep your moral integrity. Nursing has its own profession-specific code. Seen as: reporting your own error.

Autonomy and membership in a professional organization. Working under professional groups gives nursing governance, self-regulation, and legal and clinical autonomy. Seen as: joining a specialty association or practice council.
steps: Underline the behavior in the stem.
Ask what drives it: learning, evidence, serving others, doing right at a cost, or shaping standards.
Avoid traps: habit is not a body of knowledge, and paid overtime is not service orientation.
sections.example: Near the end of her shift, a nurse realizes she missed an ordered neurovascular check on a client with a new cast. She does the check now, charts the real time, and tells the charge nurse. She never charts it as done on time.

check.q: A nurse’s friend and coworker smells of alcohol and slurs words while preparing medications. What does the code of ethics require?
check.a: Protect clients first. Stop her from giving care and tell the charge nurse or supervisor right away. Friendship does not outweigh client safety.

sections.heading: Why habit is not a defense
sections.keyIdea: You cannot defend a decision based on habit; accountable nurses use current evidence and change practice through proper channels.
sections.body:
You cannot answer for a decision you cannot explain. “We have always done it this way” is not an explanation.

Education keeps you current. The ANA recommends the BSN for entry into practice. Magnet hospitals push for BSN-prepared nurses. Nursing knowledge keeps growing, so some of what you learn now will become outdated.

Evidence-based practice (EBP) brings new knowledge to the bedside. It blends research, your expertise, and the client’s values. If a unit routine conflicts with evidence, bring the evidence to the practice council or educator. Do not keep it up blindly or change it alone. If an order conflicts with evidence, clarify it with the prescriber.

Course vs current: Your course guide says Magnet hospitals require BSN-prepared nurses. Current standard: Magnet requires nurse managers and nurse leaders to hold a BSN or higher. Staff RNs do not all need a BSN, but the hospital must show a plan to raise its share of BSN staff. On a course exam, expect “Magnet requires BSN nurses.” On the NCLEX, this detail is rarely tested.
bullets: Strongest evidence: systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials.
Next: single randomized trials, then nonrandomized and observational studies.
Then: qualitative and descriptive studies.
Weakest: expert opinion and committee reports.

check.q: Which statement shows accountability for the body of knowledge? (a) “I learned it in school, so it is still right.” (b) “Policy says this, but I’ll check if the evidence changed and bring it to the council.”
check.a: (b). It follows policy while using EBP and governance to update practice.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: When two answers look alike, find the stem clue that shows who owns the decision and what the law allows.
sections.body: These pairs cause most wrong answers.

rows: Responsibility is doing the task. Accountability is answering for the judgment and result.
Standards, policy, or the board = professional. Acting within scope without waiting = individual.
If the client is choosing about their own care, it is client autonomy.
Councils, boards, professional groups = governance. Schedules and budgets = management.
Top of license vs beyond scope
Needs a medical order or a skill you lack? That is out of scope.
“The hospital allows it” never makes an illegal act legal.
Licensing and discipline = board. Ethics code and advocacy = ANA.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: The NCLEX shows a nurse in a situation and asks which action best shows accountability—it rarely asks for a definition.
sections.body: The NCLEX rarely asks for a definition. It shows a nurse in a situation. Then it asks which action shows accountability, or which statement needs more teaching. Wrong options often sound efficient or loyal. But they hand off ownership, hide information, or follow habit. Test each option with the three filters below.
bullets: Who owns it? The licensed nurse stays answerable.
Is it honest? It discloses, documents truthfully, and reports.
Is the client first, within scope? It protects the client without breaking scope.
steps: Read the stem. A nurse forgot a client’s 0900 oral antihypertensive. At 1300 the BP is 168/96. Which action best shows accountability? (A) Give it now and chart it at 0900. (B) Assess, tell the provider, follow direction, document accurately, and file an event report. (C) Double the next dose. (D) Let the oncoming nurse decide.
What is it really asking? How to own a missed dose and its effect.
Key cues. A missed dose is an omission. The high BP needs assessment.
Why the others are wrong. (A) is falsification. (C) is unsafe and needs an order. (D) hands off ownership.
The answer is (B). It assesses, tells the truth, stays in scope, and reports.
Strategy. Cross out options that hide, delay, or hand off ownership.

sections.heading: Worked case: Marcus’s busy shift
sections.keyIdea: Accountability covers the routine you question, the step you missed, and the chance to shape practice through governance.
sections.body: Marcus, a new RN, has a busy surgical shift. A coworker says the unit irrigates drains a way Marcus thinks current guidance no longer supports. He gave an IV opioid at 1400 but could not reassess until 1520 due to an admission. The client is comfortable, with pain at 3/10. The manager also asks for practice council volunteers.
steps: Cues. A routine may conflict with evidence. A required reassessment was late—an omission, even with a good outcome.
Drain routine. He follows current policy but looks up the evidence and brings it to the educator or council.
Late reassessment. IV opioids are usually reassessed in about 15–30 minutes. He reassesses now, charts the real time, and reports per policy.
Prevent a repeat. Next time, he asks the charge nurse for help when tasks clash.
Council. Joining shows component 5 and gives his drain question a proper forum.

check.q: What if the client had a respiratory rate of 8 at 1520?
check.a: Safety first: stay, stimulate, support breathing, follow the reversal or rapid response protocol, and notify the provider. Reporting comes after the client is stable.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In North Carolina, the NCBON sets nursing scope, and the RN keeps assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment.
sections.body: The NCLEX will not ask NC statute numbers. Use these facts in real NC practice.
bullets: The NC Board of Nursing (NCBON) regulates nursing under the Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq., Chapter 90, Article 9A).
RN rules are in 21 NCAC 36 .0224; LPN rules are in .0225.
The RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment. The LPN works under RN or provider supervision.
The RN delegates tasks, never the nursing process or judgment. NCBON offers scope-of-practice and UAP delegation decision trees.
Facility policy can be stricter than these rules, never broader.
NC is a Nurse Licensure Compact state; follow the practice law where the client is.
NCBON uses a Just Culture–based tool: human error, at-risk behavior, or reckless behavior.
Diversion, impairment on duty, fraud, boundary violations, and confidentiality breaches go to the Board. NCBON offers alternative-to-discipline programs.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Source: Module 42 study guide, Glossary terms 1–3 and “The Concept of Accountability & Its Five Core Components,” pp. 2703–2704. Added for NCLEX context: the four look-alike terms, shared governance, the roles of the board, NCSBN, and ANA, and evidence ranking. Where the course and current practice differ, learn both, as listed below.
bullets: Top-of-license: Your course guide says TOL is for nurses with a BSN or higher. Current standard: every nurse practices to the full extent of his or her own education and scope. On a course exam, expect the BSN wording; on the NCLEX, apply TOL to any RN.

Entry pathways: Your course guide lists diploma, ADN, BSN, MSN, and DNP/PhD as ways into practice. Current standard: first RN licensure comes through a diploma, ADN, BSN, or entry-level master’s program, plus the NCLEX-RN. On a course exam, expect the five-program list; on the NCLEX, every route ends with the NCLEX-RN.

Codes of ethics: Your course guide says codes are “regulated alongside state boards of nursing via the NCSBN.” Current standard: the ANA writes the Code; boards enforce the law and may discipline unethical conduct. On a course exam, expect the NCSBN wording; on the NCLEX, the Code belongs to the ANA.

Magnet: Your course guide says Magnet hospitals require BSN-prepared nurses. Current standard: Magnet requires a BSN or higher for nurse managers and leaders, plus a plan to grow BSN staff. On a course exam, expect “Magnet requires BSN nurses”; the NCLEX rarely tests this.
Component labels: the course calls component 1 “Education (Body of Knowledge).” It is still a separate item from component 2, Body of Knowledge.
IOM: now the National Academy of Medicine. The Future of Nursing 2020–2030 adds health equity.

mnemonics.name: Five components: “Every Brave Student Can Achieve”
mnemonics.text: Education • Body of knowledge • Service orientation • Code of ethics • Autonomy and professional organization.

mnemonics.name: Accountable answer pattern: A-A-C-D-R
mnemonics.text: Assess → Act within scope → Communicate → Document truthfully → Report and follow up. Options that skip these steps, hide information, or hand off ownership are usually wrong.

pearls: Delegate tasks, never accountability for your judgment or follow-up.
Omissions count: a missed reassessment or unreported finding is yours to answer for.
Policy can narrow scope but never expand it beyond the Nurse Practice Act.
Top of license means the full extent of your scope AND your competence—never beyond either.
Change a practice you disagree with through evidence and governance, not quiet noncompliance.
redFlags: Charting care that was not done, or at a false time, is falsification.
Co-signing a waste you did not witness enables drug diversion.
Letting an impaired coworker keep caring for clients violates your first duty to safety.
Assuming a delegated task was done right without checking results.

checks.q: A charge nurse says, “Don’t bother with an event report for that near miss—nothing happened.” What is the accountable response?
checks.a: Explain that near misses are reported so the system can learn and prevent harm. Then file the report per policy.

checks.q: A nurse who just moved says nurses at her old hospital changed doses “whenever it made sense.” What guides her now?
checks.a: The Nurse Practice Act of the state where the client is, plus current policy and protocols. Dose changes need an order or an approved protocol.

checks.q: The manager wants a client discharged now for a bed. The client, new on insulin, still cannot inject a dose correctly. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Say the client cannot inject safely yet, notify the provider, and keep teaching or arrange a safe option. Bed pressure never outweighs safety at discharge.

checks.q: A nurse serves on a specialty association’s standards committee. Which component does this show?
checks.a: Autonomy and membership in a professional organization—taking part in the governance that sets nursing standards.

checks.q: An LPN asks the RN to sign an admission assessment the LPN did alone: “You’re busy; I’ve done hundreds.” Should the RN sign it?
checks.a: No. The comprehensive admission assessment is RN work. The LPN may collect data, but the RN must assess and validate it herself. Signing work she did not do misstates her accountability.

checks.q: Why is “I followed the provider’s order exactly” not always a defense?
checks.a: The nurse is accountable for her own judgment. If an order is unclear or unsafe for this client, she must question it, clarify with the prescriber, and escalate if needed.

topics.title: Bedside Accountability: Duties, Delegation, Unsafe Orders
topics.summary: At the bedside, accountability means doing your core duties well and keeping the decisions you cannot hand off: delegating safely, questioning unsafe orders, escalating, and owning errors.
objectives: You can apply the six expanded duties to a client situation.
You can decide what to assign, delegate, or keep as the RN.
You can question an unsafe order and escalate it.
You can explain what you answer for with range orders and errors.
You can recognize mandatory reporting and screen for abuse and suicide.
You can match nursing actions to the seven related concepts in the matrix.
topics.bigPicture:
In the first lesson, accountability was a principle. Here it becomes things you do every shift. You assess comfort, screen for abuse and suicide risk, prevent infection, and teach. If you skip one, you answer for the omission.

This lesson also covers decisions under pressure. A client says “I’m fine” while shaking with pain. An LPN throws away urine that was supposed to be strained. An IV order looks unsafe for a 78-year-old. In each case the RN must assess, clarify, speak up, and document. The RN stays accountable for the outcome, even when someone else did the task or wrote the order.
recap: Six duties: wellness, physical outcomes, safety, trauma and suicide, teaching, and infection prevention.
Finish the assessment before leaving the room, especially when words and cues don’t match.
Clarify an order that conflicts with evidence or the client’s condition. Never change it yourself.
If an unsafe order stands: hold it, tell the prescriber, escalate, and document facts.
The RN stays accountable after delegating. Never delegate assessment, teaching, evaluation, or unstable clients to assistive personnel.
You answer for your process—assessing, dosing within the order, monitoring—not for a drug’s biology.
Report suspected abuse without waiting for proof. Screen every client for abuse and suicide risk.
Just Culture: console human error, coach at-risk behavior, sanction reckless behavior.

keyTerms.def: The areas a nurse answers for: wellness, physical outcomes, safety, trauma, education, and infection prevention.
A legal duty to report known or suspected abuse or neglect, and certain injuries such as gunshot wounds, to the agency named in state law.
An infection a client gets while receiving care that was not present or incubating on admission.
Letting someone perform a specific nursing task beyond their usual role. The delegating nurse keeps accountability.
Directing someone to do work within their own scope or routine role, such as an LPN caring for stable clients.
Right task, right circumstance, right person, right directions and communication, and right supervision and evaluation.
Trained, unlicensed staff, such as nursing assistants, who do assigned or delegated tasks under a nurse’s supervision.
The line of authority for an unsolved concern: prescriber, charge nurse, supervisor or manager, then medical director or chief nursing officer.
A report format: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation.
An order with a dose range, such as hydromorphone 1–4 mg IV PRN. The nurse picks the dose by assessment and policy.
A confidential quality-improvement report of an error or near miss. It is never filed in or mentioned in the chart.
A safety approach that consoles human error, coaches at-risk behavior, and disciplines reckless behavior, while fixing system causes.

sections.heading: What duties does accountability cover?
sections.keyIdea: Each duty has an assessment part and an action part, and the right exam answer often adds the skipped assessment.
sections.body:
The course says accountability governs seven areas of care. They are health and wellness needs, physical outcomes, client safety, trauma and abuse reporting, suicide prevention, client teaching, and infection control.

The course groups bedside accountability into six duties. Each has something to assess and something to do. When a question shows a skipped step, it is usually the assessment.

Take education. Before teaching, assess learning style and readiness. Keep your own knowledge current, too.

rows: Body, mind (cognitive and psychologic health), and spirit
Screenings, vaccines, quitting smoking, exercise, healthy diet, stress management; refer to counselor, clergy, or support group
Fluids, nutrition, rest and sleep, oxygenation, elimination, pain and comfort
Meet each need; manage pain before it gets severe; reassess
Hazards in the room; injury risk across the lifespan
Keep the setting hazard-free; teach injury prevention; urge clients to voice concerns
Screen every client for abuse; assess risk of self-harm, suicidal ideation, and intent
Report known or suspected abuse and reportable injuries such as gunshot wounds; suicide precautions
Learning style and readiness to learn
Teach about health, illness, tests, procedures, diagnoses, treatments, and self-care; keep up your own continuing education and EBP
Weak immunity; your own exposures and illness
Teach the public about vaccines; strict infection control, PPE, and hand hygiene to prevent healthcare-associated infections (HAIs)

check.q: A client got IV morphine 20 minutes ago, is drowsy, and says, “Just leave the warfarin papers.” Which duty is at risk?
check.a: Education. The client is not ready to learn. Teach when the client is alert, and confirm learning with teach-back.

sections.heading: What does the related-concepts matrix say?
sections.keyIdea: For each related concept, the course lists what the nurse answers for and the exact nursing actions that show it.
sections.body:
The course links seven concepts to accountability in one matrix (p. 2705). Each row names what you are accountable for. It then lists the nursing actions that prove it. Exam items often describe one of these actions and ask which concept it shows.

Comfort is the row students miss most. You assess comfort, report changes, and document both the comfort level and every intervention.

Course vs current: Your course guide says to assess comfort at least once per shift, or more often if the client’s condition calls for it. Current standard: assess pain on admission, at the intervals set by policy, with any change, and after every pain intervention. On a course exam, expect “at least once per shift.” On the NCLEX, reassess after each intervention.

rows: Assessing comfort and giving effective care to promote it
Assess comfort at least once per shift, or more often per condition; report any change; document comfort level and all interventions
Practicing in an EBP setting and using evidence in your own care
Search the literature for current evidence; choose interventions based on what it shows
Assessing current health and using teaching, care, and referrals to prevent illness

Assess biophysical, cognitive, psychologic, and spiritual health; teach general prevention (exercise, vaccines) and risk-specific changes (quit smoking, heart-healthy diet); refer to counselors, clergy, dietitians, physical therapists, support groups, and community resources
Protecting clients with weak immune systems
Check history for immune problems (autoimmune disease, cancer, chemotherapy); stay aware of your own health and use PPE; know how diseases spread; teach vaccines and hygiene
Keeping clients safe in care and teaching risk reduction for daily life
Find and fix immediate hazards; assess injury risk outside the facility; report safety concerns to supervisors per policy; teach helmet use and child safety restraints
Client teaching, staying current, and guiding preceptees and students
Assess client and family learning needs and readiness; design teaching from EBP; read current journals and attend workshops or seminars; keep competence through continuing education
Spotting abuse or violence, preventing more harm, and reporting as the law requires
Assess for physical, emotional, or sexual abuse; screen abuse and suicide risk on admission; watch for spoken or shown warning signs

check.q: A nurse checks a client’s history for chemotherapy and wears PPE. Which matrix concept is this?
check.a: Infection. The nurse is accountable for protecting clients whose immune systems are weak.

sections.heading: What if the client says “I’m fine”?
sections.keyIdea: When words and cues don’t match, believe the whole picture, finish the assessment, and keep working on the problem.
sections.body:
In the course case, new RN Jen Sturges assesses Kathryn Miller, 45. She has a GI diagnosis and a history of back pain. Ms. Miller says she is “doing just fine.” But her blood pressure is high, and she is shaking and gripping the sheets. She fears narcotics and calls pain “my enemy.” Those are signs of severe pain.

Jen must finish the assessment before leaving the room. Then she reports the findings to the charge nurse.

A competent adult may refuse an opioid. But respecting a refusal is not dropping the problem. Untreated pain raises blood pressure, slows healing, and worsens anxiety. So the nurse explores fears and corrects myths. One myth is that short-term opioid use for acute pain almost always causes addiction.
steps: Notice that the words and cues don’t match.
Finish the assessment: pain scale, nonverbal signs, vital signs, and fears.
Explore: “Tell me more about your fear of narcotics.”
Plan with the charge nurse, provider, and pharmacist (for non-opioid options safe with her GI problem).
Offer options she accepts, and respect an informed refusal.
Reassess after each step. Document comfort, her words, teaching, and interventions.

check.q: After teaching, Ms. Miller still declines all opioids. Is charting “client refuses pain medication” enough?
check.a: No. Charting is required but not enough. Offer ordered non-opioid and nondrug options, tell the provider pain is uncontrolled, and reassess soon.

sections.heading: What if an order seems unsafe?
sections.keyIdea: Clarify before you carry it out; if the prescriber won’t change an unsafe order, hold it and move up the chain of command.
sections.body:
In the course case, Frank Epworth, 78, has a suspected kidney stone. Orders include normal saline at 500 mL/hr. The nurse recalls guidance that large, fast IV fluid volumes rarely help stones pass. At 78, he also risks fluid overload.

She cannot ignore the concern because “the provider ordered it.” She also cannot change the rate on her own. She assesses him and calls the prescriber with data and evidence.

If the prescriber keeps an unsafe order, the nurse does not carry it out. That is accountability, not insubordination. Use the TeamSTEPPS tool CUS: “I am Concerned. I am Uncomfortable. This is a Safety issue.” Under the two-challenge rule, say it twice, then move up the chain. Anyone may “stop the line”—pause care—for safety.

The ANA Code of Ethics backs this up. Your primary commitment is to the client. You must protect the client’s health and safety, and you answer for your own judgments and actions. So if a prescriber refuses to change an unsafe order, refuse to carry it out. Document the conversation. Then go up the chain of command right away: charge nurse, nursing supervisor, then medical director.
steps: Assess the client. For fluids, check lungs, breathing, SpO2, edema, and intake and output.
Check facts with a guideline, drug reference, or pharmacist.
Call the prescriber using SBAR and make a clear recommendation.
If the order changes, read it back and carry it out. If it stays unsafe, hold it and tell the prescriber.
Escalate: charge nurse, supervisor or manager, then medical director or chief nursing officer.
Keep the client safe. Document who, when, what was said, and what was done.

check.q: A provider orders potassium chloride 20 mEq IV push: “Just push it slowly.” What should the nurse do?
check.a: Withhold it, tell the provider, and notify the charge nurse. IV push potassium can cause fatal dysrhythmias.

sections.heading: What can you delegate or assign?
sections.keyIdea: The task moves to someone else, but the RN’s accountability for the decision, directions, and follow-up stays put.
sections.body:
In the Epworth case, an LPN says, “He voided 30 mL. I charted it and threw it out without straining.” Is the RN accountable? Yes. The LPN answers for the task. The RN answers for the choice, the directions, and the follow-up.

The 2019 NCSBN and ANA guidelines use two terms. Assignment is work within a person’s scope or routine role, like an LPN caring for stable clients. Delegation is a specific nursing task beyond the person’s usual role, after training. The RN stays accountable in both. The steps follow the five rights.

Course vs current: Your course guide says the RN “delegates” urine straining to the LPN. Current standard: under the 2019 NCSBN and ANA guidelines, giving an LPN routine work within LPN scope is an assignment. On a course exam, expect the word “delegates.” On the NCLEX, call it an assignment. Either way, the RN stays accountable.
steps: Right circumstance: Is the client stable and predictable? If new or changing, keep the client.
Right task: Does it need assessment, planning, first teaching, evaluation, or judgment? Then keep it.
Right person: Is it in their scope or task list, allowed by policy, with skill verified?
Right directions: Say what to do and what to report right away. “Strain every void, save any stone in the labeled cup, and tell me at once about clots or new pain.”
Right supervision: Check in, review results yourself, act, and give feedback.

check.q: Which can go to a nursing assistant: teaching insulin injection, a fingerstick glucose on a stable client, or a fresh post-op assessment?
check.a: The fingerstick, if it is on the approved list and skill is verified. The others stay with the RN.

sections.heading: What do you answer for with medications?
sections.keyIdea: You are not accountable for how a drug works in the body, but you are accountable for every step of your process.
sections.body:
Mr. Epworth’s order is hydromorphone (Dilaudid) 1–4 mg IV PRN (as needed). An hour after 1 mg, his pain is still 8/10, so the nurse gives 3 mg. Is she accountable if it fails? Not for the drug’s failure. She is accountable for her process.

First, check the order and the policy on choosing a dose within a range. Assess pain, sedation, breathing, and SpO2. Older adults have higher risk of slowed breathing, so watch closely. Reassess at peak, often about 15–30 minutes for IV opioids. Call the provider if relief is poor. Sedation rises before breathing slows, so growing sleepiness is a warning.

You also own your errors. Assess and treat the client first. Then notify the provider, chart the facts, and file an event report. Never mention the report in the chart.

Just Culture judges the choice behind an error, as the table shows.

rows: Picking the wrong client from look-alike names
Skipping barcode scanning because it is slow

sections.example: Thirty minutes after 3 mg, Mr. Epworth is drowsy but easy to wake. Respirations are 14 and pain is 5/10. The nurse keeps watching and calls the provider about a non-opioid. Before any NSAID, she checks kidney function, bleeding risk, and GI history.

check.q: Is the nurse accountable for the drug failing to relieve pain, or for the 30-minute reassessment?
check.a: The reassessment and what follows. Nurses answer for a sound process, not for a client’s drug response.

sections.heading: Safety, infection, abuse, and suicide screening
sections.keyIdea: Fix hazards first, protect weak immune systems, screen privately for abuse, ask directly about suicide, and report suspicion.
sections.body:
Safety: fix an immediate hazard first, then report it. Teach prevention, such as bike helmets and child car seats.

Infection: check for weak immunity from cancer, chemotherapy, or autoimmune disease. Use PPE and teach about vaccines and hygiene. If you have a fever, tell your supervisor and employee health, and stay home.

Abuse: screen every client privately. Document objective findings and the client’s own words. Report reasonable suspicion. You need no proof, and you do not investigate. Some injuries, such as gunshot wounds, must be reported per state law even if the client objects.

Suicide: screen on admission. Ask directly, “Are you thinking about killing yourself?” Asking does not plant the idea.

Course vs current: Your course guide says nurses must report known or suspected abuse of children and older adults. Current standard: every state requires reports of suspected child abuse. Adult rules vary by state. In NC, the adult duty covers a disabled adult who needs protective services, not age alone. On a course exam, expect “children and older adults.” On the NCLEX, report suspected abuse of a child or vulnerable adult to the designated agency.

rows: Burns in a pattern that doesn’t fit the story
Keep the child safe; treat; document; report to child protective services
“Everyone would be better off without me”
Ask directly about thoughts, plan, and means; keep safe
Nurse with fever before an oncology shift
Stay home; notify supervisor and employee health

check.q: A woman with a facial bruise says she “walked into a door.” Her partner answers every question. What first?
check.a: Interview her privately with direct, caring screening questions. Safety planning and any required report follow.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Most traps hinge on who owns the decision, whether the client is stable, and whether the action is in scope.
sections.body: When two answers both sound right, use this table.

rows: Either way, the RN stays accountable. Match the task to the person and the client’s stability.
Words like evaluate, interpret, or assess mean RN work.
New symptoms or a fresh post-op client stay with the RN.
Never adjust a rate or dose on your own.
Report suspicion. Never wait for proof or confront the suspected abuser.
Never write “incident report filed” in the chart.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect delegation, unsafe-order, reporting, and error questions; the right answer protects the client and keeps judgment with the RN.
sections.body: Four question types show up often. Delegation asks which task or client fits an LPN or assistant. Unsafe orders ask what the nurse does first. Reporting asks about abuse, suicide, or reportable injuries. Errors ask who is accountable and what to document.
steps: Read the stem. “Which client should the RN assign to the LPN?” (A) Chest pain, admitted 30 minutes ago. (B) Stable chronic leg ulcer needing a scheduled dressing and routine oral meds. (C) Needs first teaching on home tube feeding. (D) Two hours after thyroidectomy with new tingling around the mouth.
What is it really asking? Which client is stable with a predictable outcome.
Key cues. “30 minutes ago,” “first teaching,” and “new tingling” mean RN work. “Stable” and “routine” fit an LPN.
Why (A) is wrong. A new chest-pain admission is not yet stable.
Why (C) is wrong. First teaching belongs to the RN.
Why (D) is wrong. Tingling after thyroid surgery suggests low calcium—an acute change.
The answer is (B). Routine care for a stable client fits LPN scope.
Strategy. Stable and routine can go to others. New, changing, teaching, or assessment stays with the RN.

sections.heading: Worked case: Dana’s night shift
sections.keyIdea: Assess the biggest physical threat first, give clear directions, and report suspected abuse without confronting anyone.
sections.body: Dana, an RN, works nights with an LPN, Rob, and an assistant, Kia. Mr. Ortiz, 81, has heart failure, crackles, and a new order for saline at 250 mL/hr. Rob has Ms. Patel, who has renal colic and an order to strain all urine. Mrs. Greene, 84, has a hip fracture and bruises of different ages on both arms. Her son answers every question and won’t leave.
steps: Prioritize. Fluid overload is the biggest threat. Dana assesses Mr. Ortiz first, then calls the provider with SBAR and suggests a lower rate.
Direct clearly. Rob strains every void and saves any stone. Kia reports Mr. Ortiz’s urine output every 2 hours and any breathing trouble at once.
Screen privately. Dana talks with Mrs. Greene alone and documents the bruises and her words.

Report. She tells the provider and charge nurse and reports to adult protective services per state law (in NC, county DSS under G.S. 108A-102 if she is a disabled adult needing protective services). She does not confront the son or wait for proof.
Evaluate. She rechecks Mr. Ortiz and follows up on the report.

check.q: At 0300, Rob says he forgot to strain one void. Who is accountable?
check.a: Both. Rob answers for his work; Dana answers for supervision and the outcome. She reinforces directions, tells the provider if it matters, documents, and gives feedback without blame—a human error.

sections.heading: Worked case: Ms. Miller’s hidden pain
sections.keyIdea: Finish the assessment, trust the cues over “I’m fine,” report the full picture, and keep working when a client refuses pain medicine.
sections.body:
This is the course’s Case Study Part 1 (p. 2704). New RN Jen Sturges assesses Kathryn Miller, 45. She was admitted with a GI diagnosis and has a history of back pain. The nursing assistant (CNA) took her blood pressure, and it is high.

Ms. Miller says she is “doing just fine.” But she is shaking, very anxious, and gripping the bed sheets tightly. She fears narcotics. She says she “refuses to pay attention to my body” and that “pain is my enemy.” Work through the five course questions below.
steps: Q1. Why finish the assessment before leaving the room? A full assessment catches subtle body and behavior cues, such as high BP, shaking, and guarding. That prevents missed decline. It also meets Jen’s duty to get accurate baseline data and manage comfort.
Q2. What other symptoms does Jen see? High blood pressure (taken by the CNA), extreme anxiety, shaking, tight gripping of the sheets, and spoken denial or avoidance of pain (“pain is my enemy”).

Q3. What should Jen tell the charge nurse? The high BP, the nonverbal signs of severe pain (shaking, gripping sheets), her fear of narcotic side effects, her back pain history, and her GI diagnosis. Then they can plan safe, tailored pain care.

Q4. Who should they work with? The primary healthcare provider (HCP) or hospitalist. The clinical pharmacist, to review non-narcotic or multimodal pain drugs that are safe with her GI problem. Possibly a pain management specialist or a physical or integrative therapist.

Q5. Why not just accept the refusal? Untreated pain causes harmful stress responses: high BP, slower healing, and more anxiety. Accountability for comfort means exploring her fears, teaching about non-opioid and nondrug options, and advocating for safe relief. Accepting the refusal and walking away abandons the problem.

check.q: Ms. Miller says she is fine, but she is shaking and gripping the sheets. What should Jen do before leaving the room?
check.a: Finish the assessment, including a pain rating, nonverbal signs, vital signs, and her fears. Then report the full picture to the charge nurse.

sections.heading: Worked case: Mr. Epworth’s kidney stone
sections.keyIdea: The RN answers for delegation choices, her own medication process, and questioning orders that conflict with evidence.
sections.body:
This is the course’s Case Study 2 (p. 2710). Frank Epworth, 78, is admitted with a suspected kidney stone (urolithiasis). He has severe left flank and back pain, nausea and vomiting, and blood in the urine (hematuria).

Orders: Dilaudid (hydromorphone) 1–4 mg IV PRN for pain, normal saline IV at 500 mL/hr, and strain all urine. The RN gives Dilaudid 1 mg IV. She hands urine collection and straining to an LPN. Work through the three course questions below.
steps: Q1. Thirty minutes later, the LPN says he voided 30 mL five minutes ago. She charted it and threw it out without straining. Is the RN accountable? Yes. The LPN answers for doing the task right. The RN keeps overall accountability for outcomes, choosing to hand off the task, clearly stating the key instruction (strain for stone analysis), and supervising and evaluating the care.

Q2. An hour after the first dose, pain is 8/10 with no relief. The RN gives 3 mg more per the order. Is she accountable if it fails? No, not for the drug failing. That holds if she assessed well, gave a dose within the 1–4 mg range safely, and monitored him. She is accountable for reassessing pain afterward and calling the HCP if the plan still fails.

Q3. After starting the IV, she recalls guidance that large fluid pushes rarely help stones pass. What now? Accountability for EBP and safety applies. He is 78, and 500 mL/hr risks fluid overload. She questions the order, calls the prescriber to share the evidence, and advocates for a safer, evidence-based rate.

check.q: Is the RN accountable when the LPN throws away unstrained urine?
check.a: Yes. The LPN answers for the task, but the RN answers for the handoff decision, the clear directions, and the follow-up.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In NC, the RN delegates tasks, not judgment, and anyone who suspects child maltreatment must report it to county DSS.
sections.body: Use these NC facts in real practice. The NCLEX tests the national rule: report suspicion to the designated agency.
bullets: Under 21 NCAC 36 .0224 (RN) and .0225 (LPN), the RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment. NCBON publishes a Decision Tree for Delegation to UAP.
Nurse Aide I registry: NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation. Nurse Aide II registry: NCBON. NA II must also be on the NA I registry.
NA II tasks include some sterile and advanced tasks, such as sterile dressings and oxygen. The task must be on the list and right for this client.

Children (G.S. 7B-301): anyone who suspects a juvenile under 18 is abused, neglected, or dependent, or died from maltreatment, must report to the county DSS director. Knowingly not reporting is a crime.

Disabled adults (G.S. 108A-102): anyone with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult needs protective services must report to county DSS. Older adults are covered when they meet this definition. Report suspicion; do not investigate.
Good-faith reporters are immune. A hospital’s internal process does not replace your duty to make sure DSS gets the report.
Diversion, impairment, fraud, boundary violations, and confidentiality breaches go to the Board.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Source: Module 42 study guide, “The Concept of Accountability” intro and “Expanded Duties Under Accountability” (pp. 2703–2704), the Nursing Implications Matrix (p. 2705), Case Study 1: Ms. Kathryn Miller (p. 2704), Case Study 2: Mr. Frank Epworth (p. 2710), and “Linking Accountability to Ethics” (p. 2710). Added: NCSBN/ANA (2019) delegation guidelines, CUS, SBAR, and Just Culture.
bullets: Delegation vs assignment: Your course guide says the RN “delegates” straining to an LPN. Current standard: under the 2019 NCSBN/ANA guidelines, that is an assignment. On a course exam, expect “delegates”; on the NCLEX, call it an assignment. The RN is accountable either way.

Comfort checks: Your course guide says assess comfort at least once per shift, or more often per condition. Current standard: also assess on admission, with changes, and after each intervention (about 15–30 minutes for IV and 30–60 minutes for oral). On a course exam, expect “at least once per shift”; on the NCLEX, reassess after every intervention.

Reporting: Your course guide says report abuse of “children and older adults.” Current standard: child reporting is universal, but adult rules vary by state (in NC, disabled adults who need protective services). On a course exam, expect “children and older adults”; on the NCLEX, report suspected abuse of a child or vulnerable adult to the designated agency.
Hydromorphone: 3 mg an hour after 1 mg is fine only if the order’s frequency and policy allow.
Unsafe orders: also tell the prescriber you are holding it, and keep monitoring.

mnemonics.name: Five rights: “Tasks Can Pass Down Safely”
What the RN keeps: “EAT”
mnemonics.text: Evaluate • Assess • Teach—plus any unstable client.

pearls: “I delegated it” is never a full answer. You own the choice and the follow-up.
Unsafe orders are never made safe by documenting them or handing them to another nurse.
Screen for abuse privately, and ask about suicide directly.
Event reports never go in the chart; chart only the facts of care.
redFlags: A high IV fluid rate in an older client with heart failure: assess for overload and clarify the order.
Growing sleepiness after an opioid, even with a normal breathing rate, warns of respiratory depression.
Delegating the care of a client whose condition is changing to assistive personnel.
Injuries that don’t fit the story, or a caregiver who won’t leave.
A client who says others would be “better off without me.”

checks.q: A 15-year-old has a spiral arm fracture, and the parent says the child fell off the couch. Must the nurse have proof before reporting?
checks.a: No. Report reasonable suspicion to child protective services (in NC, county DSS) and document objectively.

checks.q: A nurse forgot a glucose check before insulin, and the client is now shaky and sweaty. Event report or client first?
checks.a: The client. Check glucose, treat per protocol, and notify the provider. Then file the event report.

checks.q: An NC Nurse Aide II may do sterile dressings. Today the wound has new pus and the client has a fever. Delegate it?
checks.a: No. The client has changed and needs RN assessment. The task must be allowed and right for this client today.

checks.q: A nurse routinely skips barcode scanning because it is slow. What is the Just Culture response?
checks.a: Coaching. This is at-risk behavior, a drift into an unsafe shortcut whose risk is underestimated.

checks.q: An assistant reports a client’s BP is 182/104 with a new headache. The RN is mid-dressing change on another client. Best action?
checks.a: Arrange cover for the dressing if it can’t be paused safely, assess the client yourself, and notify the provider. The assistant cannot interpret or act on the finding.

topics.title: Competence: Critical Thinking, Benner, and Your Limits
topics.summary: Competence is using specialized knowledge, skills, and judgment to give safe care, and it always includes knowing your limits and asking for help.
objectives: You can explain how competence and accountability depend on each other.
You can spot critical thinking, emotional intelligence, and ethical reasoning in a nurse’s actions.
You can place a nurse in one of Benner’s five stages.
You can apply the first rule of competence: ask for help when unsure.
You can respond safely when floated to a unit beyond your skills.
You can name the core elements of cultural and lifelong competence.
topics.bigPicture:
Competence is the bridge between knowing and doing. A competent nurse uses knowledge, skills, and judgment to give safe care. The course also says competence includes “awareness of personal capabilities and limitations.” The safest nurse is not the one who never asks. It is the one who knows when to ask.

You can only be accountable for care you are able to give. So taking on work you can’t do safely is itself an accountability failure. On the NCLEX, competence shows up in floating, new graduates, fatigue, double-checks, emotions clouding judgment, and culturally responsive care.
recap: Competence is knowledge, skills, and judgment, plus awareness of your limits and openness to feedback.
Three core areas: critical thinking, problem solving with emotional intelligence, and ethical reasoning.
Benner: novice, advanced beginner, competent (2–3 years), proficient (3–5 years), expert. Stage is setting-specific.
First rule of competence: always ask for help when unsure whether an action is safe.
Even experts double-check high-alert medications and sterile processes.
Floated beyond your skills? Speak up before report, decline an independent assignment, and negotiate a safe role.
Fatigue, illness, and impairment make a skilled nurse unsafe; fitness for duty is part of competence.
Cultural competence means asking the person, using trained interpreters, and never stereotyping.

keyTerms.def: Practicing to the fullest extent with specialized knowledge, skills, abilities, and judgment, while knowing your limits and staying open to feedback.
Careful, evidence-based reasoning. Critical thinkers stay open to others, know their limits, and investigate before acting.
Applying classroom theory to real clinical situations so knowledge becomes usable judgment.
Working through a clinical problem to a solution. It grows with practice and EBP and depends on self-awareness.

Using emotional appraisal to notice when your own emotions, not objective data, are steering a clinical decision. It builds strong working relationships with clients and peers and supports self-aware problem solving.
Using ethical principles and the ANA Code in everyday decisions, respecting client preferences, and checking your own fitness to practice.
Being physically and mentally able to practice safely—not exhausted, ill, impaired, or overwhelmed.
Patricia Benner’s five levels of skill: novice, advanced beginner, competent, proficient, and expert.
A short rule of thumb from experience, such as “if X happens, see the client now.” Proficient nurses use them.
Always ask for help whenever you are unsure an action is safe. “I don’t know” is safer than guessing.
A second nurse separately verifies a high-alert drug, dose, or pump setting before it is given.
Working on a unit other than your home unit to meet staffing needs. Accept only work within your competence.
Leaving clients you have accepted without a proper handoff to another qualified nurse.
Giving care that respects a client’s cultural values, beliefs, and practices, built on self-awareness, listening, advocacy, and community resources.
Preventable gaps in health outcomes between groups of people.

sections.heading: What is competence?
sections.keyIdea: Competence means you can give the care safely—and you know where your skills end.
sections.body:
Competence is practicing to the fullest extent with specialized knowledge, skills, and judgment. A competent nurse uses three core areas: critical thinking, problem solving, and ethical reasoning. She also knows her limits and stays open to feedback.

Accountability says, “I answer for my care.” Competence says, “I can give that care safely.” A nurse who is accountable but not competent is a danger. A nurse who is competent but not accountable is unreliable.

Competence is not earned once. It changes with each new unit, tool, and guideline. A nurse can be an expert in labor and delivery and a beginner in the NICU on the same day. Clients trust that their nurse is prepared. Safe units protect that trust by welcoming questions, teamwork, error reporting, and ongoing education.
sections.analogy: A safe car driver is not automatically safe driving a loaded semi-truck on an icy mountain road. A good driver knows when the vehicle or road is beyond her experience and asks for help.

check.q: A nurse with 12 years in adult ICU gets her first pediatric oncology client and says, “I can handle anything.” What is missing?
check.a: Awareness of her limits. Expertise in one area does not transfer to a new population. She should name the gap and seek a mentor or resources.

sections.heading: How do critical thinking and EI work?
sections.keyIdea: Critical thinkers investigate before acting, and emotionally intelligent nurses notice when feelings, not data, are driving a choice.
sections.body:
Critical thinking starts in school and grows through situational learning—using theory in real situations. Critical thinkers stay open to others but rely on evidence. They know their limits. They investigate before acting. Giving a 0900 blood pressure pill without checking a BP of 88/52 is task completion, not thinking.

Problem solving means working through a real clinical problem. The course says it needs self-awareness and emotional intelligence (EI). EI is noticing, through emotional appraisal, when your emotions, not the facts, are shaping a decision. Feelings like concern or unease can be useful. They become dangerous when they replace data.

EI does two more jobs, per the course. It builds strong working relationships with clients and with interprofessional peers. It is also a key part of the self-awareness that problem solving needs. Problem solving matters most in complex clinical settings. It develops over time through EBP and clinical practice.

rows: Assess pain with a scale and objective signs
“I don’t want to bother the doctor again.”
Call with SBAR; escalate if needed
“She reminds me of my grandma; she can’t be worse.”
Assess new chest pressure right away

sections.example: A daughter says, “Mom is never this confused.” The chart says baseline dementia. A critical thinker does not dismiss her. She checks vital signs, SpO2, glucose, recent medications, and signs of infection, then reports the acute change.

check.q: A nurse realizes she has avoided a hostile client’s room for two hours. What shows EI?
check.a: Admit to herself that discomfort is driving the delay, assess the client now (with help if safety is a concern), and talk with the charge nurse about strategies.

sections.heading: Why is fitness for duty part of competence?
sections.keyIdea: Ethical reasoning guides everyday choices, and a tired, sick, or impaired nurse is not competent to practice at that moment.
sections.body:
Ethical reasoning uses the ANA Code of Ethics in every setting, not just the ICU or hospice. It covers telling the truth, respecting refusals, dividing your time fairly, and speaking up about unsafe shortcuts. A competent nurse respects client preferences. She does not push her own values on a client’s informed choice.

Ethical competence also means watching your own physical and emotional well-being. A skilled nurse who is exhausted, ill, impaired, or overwhelmed is not safe right then. Tell the supervisor and decline extra hours before an error happens.
bullets: Autonomy: respect the client’s right to decide.
Beneficence: do good.
Nonmaleficence: avoid harm.
Justice: be fair.
Fidelity: keep promises.
Veracity: tell the truth.
sections.example: A nurse is asked to stay for a second shift. She has been awake 20 hours and nearly scanned the wrong wristband. She tells the supervisor she is too tired to be safe and offers to stay briefly for a safe handoff.

check.q: Is ethical reasoning only for ICU, hospice, or ethics committees?
check.a: No. It is needed in every setting, every day.

sections.heading: What are Benner’s five stages?
sections.keyIdea: Nurses move from following rules to seeing the whole picture by experience, and the stage depends on the setting.
sections.body:
Patricia Benner’s model (Benner, 2001; course Box 42.3), From Novice to Expert, shows how experience builds skill. Nurses move from relying on rules to relying on experience. A novice needs rules because she can’t yet tell what matters. An expert sees the whole picture and acts smoothly.

Stages are setting-specific. A cardiac expert who moves to pediatrics may be an advanced beginner there. That is why nurses need orientation when they change specialty. A new graduate still needs help setting priorities, so a preceptor should not leave her alone with the most unstable client.

rows: Limited, inflexible performance; strictly governed by context-free rules and regulations, not experience
New graduate or early clinical exposure
Marginally acceptable performance; recognizes meaningful recurring parts of real situations from prior experience; needs help to prioritize
Strong organizing and planning; sorts important from less important factors; coordinates many complex care demands
Sees situations as wholes, not parts; uses maxims as guides; holistic understanding improves decisions; focuses on long-term goals like discharge
Fluid, flexible, highly proficient; no longer needs rules, guidelines, or maxims; uses skilled intuitive and analytic ability (“it felt right”); still double-checks high-risk actions

check.q: A nurse with 4 years on one oncology unit says, “If a neutropenic client acts even a little off, I treat it as sepsis.” She plans discharge needs early. Which stage?
check.a: Proficient. She sees the whole, uses a maxim, and focuses on long-term goals.

sections.heading: What if a task is beyond you?
sections.keyIdea: Say “I don’t know,” ask for help, and raise competence gaps before you accept an assignment.
sections.body:
The course safety alert has three rules for every level of skill. First, even experts double-check high-risk actions, like medication doses and sterilization. Independent double-checks for high-alert drugs, such as heparin, insulin drips, chemotherapy, and PCA settings, are a safeguard, not an insult. Second, saying “I don’t know” is always safer than guessing. Third, the first rule of competence: ask for help whenever you are unsure an action is safe.

Say it out loud. The course says it is always more honorable and safe to say “I don’t know” or ask “Would you help me?” than to say “I’m not sure, but I think this is right” or “I’ll figure it out as I go along.” This holds at every level of skill.

The course’s floating case, Tyree Campbell, is worked through below. Timing matters. Raise concerns before taking report. Leaving accepted clients without a handoff can be abandonment. Accepting work beyond your skill also risks malpractice claims and board discipline.
steps: Compare the assignment with your training and validated skills.
Tell the charge nurse or supervisor before report, naming the specific gap.
Show willingness to help and give the safety reason.
Offer options: tasks within your skills, a buddy role, or a unit where you are competent.
If pressed, use the chain of command and document the concern.
Once you accept clients, never leave without a proper handoff.

rows: “I’m not sure, but I think this dose is right.”
“This dose looks unusual. I’ll check with the pharmacist first.”
“I’ll figure the new pump out as I go.”
“I haven’t been trained on this pump. Will you help me and check my settings?”
“I’ve done this a hundred times; no second check needed.”
“It’s a high-alert drug, so let’s do an independent double-check.”

sections.example: Tyree says: “I want to help, but I have never worked in the NICU. I can’t safely take a full assignment. I can help with basic tasks alongside a NICU nurse, or float to mother-baby, where I’m competent.”

check.q: A charge nurse tells Tyree, “Just take the two most stable babies.” Is that acceptable?
check.a: Not as an independent assignment. Even stable NICU babies need skills she lacks. A supportive role beside a NICU nurse is acceptable.

sections.heading: What are cultural and lifelong competence?
sections.keyIdea: Culturally competent nurses ask instead of assume, use trained interpreters, and keep learning their whole careers.
sections.body:
Minority and ethnic groups are growing to become the majority of the US population. So every nurse must give culturally sensitive care. The IOM’s 2002 report Unequal Treatment linked health disparities partly to providers’ lack of cultural understanding. Other causes included language barriers, low education, poor social support, lack of insurance, poor housing, and biased attitudes. So cultural competence is part of competence.

The course lists four core elements, shown below. In practice, ask “What matters to you and your family?” Use a trained medical interpreter, not family. Facts about a group are a starting point for questions, not a prediction about one person. Cultural humility adds lifelong self-reflection.

Lifelong competence comes from continuing education, workshops, journals, certification, mentoring, and supervised orientation. Nurses must keep current, disclose skill limits, and report errors honestly.
bullets: Recognize your own values and beliefs and how they affect care.
Listen well and learn cultural rites and traditions.
Advocate for the client’s wishes when treatment conflicts with their values, especially at end of life or in psychiatric care.
Find community resources for follow-up to prevent readmission.

check.q: Before surgery, a client with limited English has her 12-year-old son offer to interpret. What is the competent action?
check.a: Thank him and get a qualified medical interpreter. A child may interpret wrongly, privacy is lost, and it burdens the child.

sections.heading: Why must competence last a whole career?
sections.keyIdea: Competence is never finished: the law requires it, ethics demands it, and you build it with ongoing learning.
sections.body:
Competence keeps growing across a nurse’s whole career. Guidelines, drugs, and devices change. So a skill that was current five years ago may not be safe today. The course links lifelong competence to the law and to ethics.

Legal link. State boards of nursing and Nurse Practice Acts require you to practice safely within your scope and your verified competence. Taking an assignment beyond your skill level exposes you to malpractice claims and board discipline.

Ethical link. You have a moral duty to keep up your competence. Be honest about what you cannot do. Remember the first rule of competence: ask for help. Report errors openly. Keep learning so the public gets safe, high-quality care.
bullets: Ways competence grows (course list): formal education, seminars, peer-reviewed journals, employer classes, and interprofessional collaboration.
Ways to close a gap in one area: continuing education, workshops, peer-reviewed literature, mentorship or preceptorship, and supervised clinical orientation.
Supportive unit culture: it encourages questions, teamwork, error reporting, and lifelong education.
Why it matters to clients: competence reassures the public that their nurse is prepared.

check.q: A nurse has not hung a blood transfusion in four years. What is the accountable step?
check.a: Tell the charge nurse about the gap and ask for a review or supervised practice before doing it. Then keep it current with education.

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Read precisely: stage vs concept, intuition vs skipped checks, and declining before report vs abandoning after.
sections.body: These confusions cost the most points on competence questions.

rows: The stage is level III (2–3 years). The concept applies to every nurse.
Competent plans and organizes. Proficient sees the whole and uses maxims.
Student = novice. New graduate = advanced beginner.
Any option where an expert skips a double-check is wrong.
Declining before report is fine. Leaving accepted clients without handoff is abandonment.
Empathy is feeling with the client. EI is noticing your own emotions steering you.
Ask the person. Never assume from ethnicity or religion.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: The right answer names the gap to the right person and gets help, training, or reassignment for that task.
sections.body: Common shapes: a nurse is floated or assigned outside her experience. A new nurse makes a statement that may need more teaching. A nurse’s emotions or fatigue threaten safety. Or a nurse’s behavior matches a Benner stage.
steps: Read the stem. A med-surg RN floated to pediatrics has a 4-year-old on a smart pump she has never used. Best action? (A) Read the manual during the shift and program the next bag. (B) Tell the charge nurse she isn’t trained on this pump and ask for help or validation. (C) Ask the parent how the pump works. (D) Decline the whole assignment.
What is it really asking? How to handle one specific skill gap.
Key cues. “Never used,” a child’s continuous infusion (high risk), and “best.”
Why (A) is wrong. It is “figure it out as I go”—the unsafe choice.
Why (C) is wrong. The parent is not responsible for device safety.
Why (D) is wrong. The gap is one device. Leaving ignores staffing needs and may be abandonment.
The answer is (B). It names the gap and gets help first.
Strategy. Reject guessing, self-teaching on the fly, shifting duty to family, and total refusal when a narrower fix exists.

sections.heading: Worked case: Aisha’s tense evening
sections.keyIdea: Name the emotion, assess the symptomatic client, admit your limits, and insist on required double-checks.
sections.body: Aisha is a new graduate in week 8 of orientation on telemetry. Her preceptor, Lou, has 15 years’ experience. Mr. Burke called her “useless” earlier. Now his monitor shows a new rhythm that may be atrial fibrillation, and he feels “fluttery.” Aisha doesn’t want to go back in. The charge nurse asks her to take a fifth client on a heparin drip. Lou says, “I barely double-check heparin anymore.”
steps: EI. Aisha names her feeling and sets it aside. A new rhythm with symptoms comes first. She assesses him, gets a rhythm strip, and calls the provider.
Benner. As an advanced beginner, she may need help with priorities. She says she can’t safely add a fifth client on heparin without help.
First rule. “I haven’t managed heparin alone yet. Will you help and do a double-check?”
Preceptor. “Policy requires an independent double-check for heparin, so let’s do it together.”
Evaluate. The rhythm is treated. The new client goes to an experienced nurse or is co-managed with a documented double-check.

check.q: Which action shows EI, and which shows the first rule of competence?
check.a: EI: seeing that her reluctance came from emotion and assessing him anyway. First rule: telling Lou she hadn’t managed heparin alone and asking for help.

sections.heading: Worked case: Tyree Campbell floats to the NICU
sections.keyIdea: A nurse must self-assess, name her limits before report, decline work she cannot do safely, and offer help within her competence.
sections.body:
This is the course’s Case Study 3 (p. 2712). Tyree Campbell is a labor and delivery (L&D) RN with 8 years of experience. L&D census is low, so she is asked to float to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU). She panics. She has never worked in the NICU.

Course vs current: Your course guide says Ms. Campbell must refuse the NICU assignment. Current standard: she declines a full, independent NICU assignment before taking report, explains the gap, and negotiates a safe role. On a course exam, “refuse” the full assignment is correct. On the NCLEX, pick the answer that tells the supervisor and offers a safe option, never walking off the unit.
steps: Q1. What is her responsibility? She is professionally and legally responsible for self-assessing her competence. She must not accept tasks or assignments she lacks the knowledge and skill for. She tells the nursing supervisor about her limits right away to protect the newborns.

Q2. Can she agree to float if she is not competent? No, not to an independent NICU assignment. That would break competence standards, the ANA Code of Ethics, and the state Nurse Practice Act. It would put critically ill newborns at high risk. She may float to do basic, non-specialized support tasks within her skills, if both agree.

Q3. What should she say? Speak respectfully, clearly, and assertively: “I want to help with staffing, but I have never worked in the NICU. I don’t have the training to safely care for critically ill newborns. I can’t take a full NICU assignment. I’m happy to help with basic tasks in my scope, or float to postpartum or mother-baby, where I am competent.”
sections.example: Short version: Tyree Campbell, a labor and delivery (L&D) nurse of 8 years, is floated to the NICU. She has never worked there. She must self-assess, tell the supervisor right away, and decline an independent NICU assignment. Taking it would break competence standards, the ANA Code, and the Nurse Practice Act. If she and the supervisor agree, she may do basic tasks within her skills.

check.q: Tyree has 8 years of L&D experience. Does that make her safe to take NICU clients?
check.a: No. Competence is setting-specific. In the NICU she has no experience, so she must name the gap and take only work within her skills.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In NC, accepting an assignment is a professional decision you answer for, and Good Samaritan protection excludes paid work.
sections.body: These NC facts help in real practice. The NCLEX rule is national: practice within your competence.
bullets: NCBON regulates nursing under G.S. 90-171.19 et seq., with RN and LPN rules in 21 NCAC 36 .0224 and .0225.
Accepting an assignment is a decision the nurse is accountable for. When floated, use the NCBON scope-of-practice decision tree, agency policy, and your validated skills.
NC is a Nurse Licensure Compact state; follow the practice law where the client is.
Malpractice claims generally must be filed within 3 years, with a 4-year statute of repose (G.S. 1-15(c)). NC keeps pure contributory negligence as a defense.
Good Samaritan (G.S. 90-21.14): protects unpaid emergency aid unless there is gross negligence, wanton conduct, or intentional wrongdoing. It does not cover your paid shift.
Impairment on duty is reported to NCBON. NCBON offers alternative-to-discipline programs for substance use.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Source: Module 42 study guide, pp. 2710–2712. This includes Glossary terms 4–5, Exemplar 42.A (learning outcomes, three core areas, and Benner’s model), Box 42.3, the Safety Alert, and Focus on Diversity and Culture. It also includes Case Study 3: Tyree Campbell and “Linking Competence to Legal Issues/Ethics” (p. 2712). Added: ethical principles, double-checks, abandonment, interpreters, and cultural humility.
bullets: Floating: Your course guide says Ms. Campbell should “refuse” the NICU assignment. Current standard: raise the concern before report, decline the independent assignment, and negotiate a safe role; leaving accepted clients without handoff may be abandonment. On a course exam, expect “refuse”; on the NCLEX, choose telling the supervisor and offering a safe option.

Benner: the course cites Benner (2001), the commemorative edition of From Novice to Expert, first published in 1984. The year ranges (2–3 and 3–5 years) are approximate and apply to the same or a similar setting.
IOM: now the National Academy of Medicine. Cultural humility and qualified interpreters are added as current standards.

mnemonics.name: Benner: “Nurses Always Climb Proudly Upward”
mnemonics.text: Novice → Advanced beginner → Competent → Proficient → Expert (rules → patterns → planning → the whole picture → intuition).

mnemonics.name: Floating script: HELP
mnemonics.text: Help offered • Explain the gap • List the safety reason • Propose options.

pearls: The safest nurse is the one who asks.
Competence is setting-specific: an expert in one area can be a novice in another.
Raise competence concerns before report; after accepting clients, hand off before leaving.
An expert’s “something isn’t right” is a valid cue to investigate and confirm with data.
redFlags: A nurse saying “I’ll figure it out as I go” about a high-risk action.
Taking an independent assignment in a specialty without training or orientation.
A preceptor skipping a required double-check.
Using a client’s child or relative to interpret medical information.
Delaying care to a client because of your own frustration or intimidation.

checks.q: A nursing student says, “I follow the checklist exactly; I don’t know yet when to adapt.” Which stage, and is this okay?
checks.a: Novice. Relying on rules is expected at this stage. The student should ask the instructor when things differ.

checks.q: A float nurse realizes after report that a client needs tracheostomy care she has never done. What should she do?
checks.a: Keep the client safe, tell the charge nurse, and ask a competent nurse to do or supervise the task. She does not attempt it alone or leave her clients.

checks.q: A med-surg nurse moves to outpatient dialysis. What plan builds competence best?
checks.a: A supervised orientation with a preceptor and competency validation before independent practice.

checks.q: A Muslim client declines a pork-derived heparin product. What is the culturally competent response?
checks.a: Respect and explore the concern, tell the provider and pharmacist so alternatives can be considered, and document.

checks.q: An expert says, “Something isn’t right with Mr. Jensen,” though his vital signs are normal. What should the team do?
checks.a: Take it seriously: reassess trends and mental status, notify the provider, and consider a rapid response if warranted.
